rules.name: Herculean Appetite
rules.text: You have a grand and terrible need that pushes you to greater heights and deeper depths. Say what it is now — Appetite:   Examples include: fame and glory, mortal pleasures, power over others, riches and property, the pride of my ancestors, the thrill of chaos, utter destruction.  You have the additional Condition, Unsatisfied. It can be marked, locked, and cleared the same as any Condition, and Reach Your Limit only triggers when it has also been marked. While Unsatisfied is marked, you have dis to all Move rolls that don’t pursue satisfaction of your appetite.  Whenever you look to satisfy your appetite, ask the GM how to pursue it here and now; they will tell you, usually with a risk or cost. When you satiate it, clear Unsatisfied. If locked, it only clears if you gratuitously overindulge it, usually with extreme cost and/or risk.

# Running the Game 

## Behind the Screen 

Running a TTRPG session can be hard; anybody who’s ever done it knows that. But it doesn't have to be, which is why we added so much to this section. One of the biggest strengths of this style of game (PbtA) is its inherent flexibility and freedom, and we want this section to leverage those strengths and make Dungeon World 2 as easy and fun to run as possible.

While previous sections of these rules are in the style of an instruction manual, this one is more like a letter and toolbox from us, as designers, to you, the GM. You want to have great experiences at the table, and we want to help, so let's talk about what we think that means.

There are also lots of tools in this chapter, meant to help both in-the-moment improvisation and structured preparation. Please pick and choose which ones you want to use. While some may reference each other, they're mostly standalone in nature.

Thank you for running this game for your friends, family, or even strangers! We sincerely hope that everything you find here helps you to have the most enjoyment while orchestrating, encouraging, and growing your Players’ fun. Dungeon World 2 truly couldn’t exist without you!

—Helena & Spencer

## The Role of the GM 

Being a Game Master (GM) is an important part of the game, and it can be extremely fun and rewarding, but it can also be nerve-wracking when first starting out (or even after decades of experience). To help ease those pressures, here is our list of what a GM is and (more importantly) isn't responsible for:

 You are responsible for portraying the world around the PCs, such as the environment, NPCs, enemies, and obstacles all along the way.
 Your NPCs are NOT the protagonists. They can still be awesome, some can be around frequently, but their most memorable moments should draw the game's focus back to the PCs in some way.
 You are NOT responsible for everyone’s fun. This is a collaborative game, and everyone is equally responsible for being mature, kind, and respectful to each other.
 You are here to have fun too! Collaboration is a two-way street, so feel free to inject your ideas into the world, or suggest an idea to a Player (after asking if they are okay with you doing so, of course).
 You are NOT the “author of a story”. This is a shared game about an evolving conversation that creates something like a story ex post facto. If you go in with a fixed “plot” in mind, then we assure you everything will become more difficult and less fun for everyone. Lean into the unexpected and let yourself be surprised. PLAY TO FIND OUT!
 You are NOT the organizer. It’s up to everyone in the group to decide how to handle things like session scheduling, group behavior, snacks, and what to do if someone is late or can’t make it. Don’t overburden yourself with these tasks, and learn to delegate them as much as possible.
 You are NOT infallible, so don’t sweat over the small stuff. If you make a mistake, or have trouble coming up with ideas, that’s okay. Feel free to ask for help from others in your gaming group, or outside of it.

## Play Order Flowchart 

This showcases what the flow of a game of Dungeon World 2 typically looks like, in more detailed fashion than in the Playing the Game section, and focused on the GM’s side of things.

1. You as the GM make a Move. Following the game’s Principles, you set up a situation. Then you usually ask “What do you do?”
2. Player(s) describe their response. Sometimes you or another Player might ask clarifying questions about this response, such as “What does it look like when you do that?” or “What do you want to accomplish?”
3. Is a Move triggered? If so, proceed to #3. If not, go back to #1.
4. Is there a roll involved? If not, resolve the Move and then go back to the start. If so, roll what the Move says. Freely remind the PCs they can Aɪᴅ each other. Also, remember that Conditions affect rolls.
5. What was the roll’s result? Follow what the Move says happens.

 A 10 or higher (10+) means a full success, as close to clean as can be expected
 A 7, 8, or 9 (7-9) is still a success but messier, with a cost, drawback, or milder consequence
 A 6 or lower (6-) means things go badly. Most of the time that means the GM makes a Move and the rolling Player gains XP, but a few Moves say something else.

1. What now? After every Move’s resolved you need to update the fiction to reflect the change that happened.
2. Has any PC marked all Conditions or reached 0 HP? If so, they Reach Their Limit (for Conditions) or Face Death (if they reached 0 HP).
3. Go back to #1!

## Agenda 

These are the core overarching goals you have while running a game of Dungeon World 2. Even if you forget or miss other parts of this chapter, the Agenda is what you should refer to when in need of guidance. Your Agenda every session is:

 Fill the Player Characters' lives with adventure
 Play to find out what happens
 Portray a meaningful fantasy world

bondTexts.champions: Your Cause: (e.g. no monarchs, protect the innocent, share your faith, etc.) One Vision. When you End the Session also ask, “Did we significantly support our cause?” If “Yes”, both of you mark 1 XP. Return the Favor. When you help or save a relevant NPC, they now support your Cause. Once in the campaign per helped/saved NPC you may request their aid; they will appear as soon as possible and help you with any current predicament you’re in. You Cannot Kill an Idea. When you Face Death while fighting for your Cause, you may choose to Go Out in a Blaze of Glory without dying. Each of you can use this Move once in a campaign. United We Stand. Each of you, once per session, may Aid the other while pursuing your Cause without paying any cost. When either of you Sense Motive, you can always ask “Do you believe in my cause?” no matter the result.
bondTexts.comrades-in-arms: Back to Back. When you Aid your comrade when they Trade Blows, you may choose one (or none): Suffer 1 dmg #piercing instead of another Aid a PC cost Instead of granting adv to their roll, you may add your dmg to theirs. This dmg is still affected by min and max choices. Killer Combo. ✷On a 12+ when you Trade Blows with your comrade's Aid, make an additional choice from the ✷10+ list. Let It All Out. When you Comfort or Support your comrade by dueling, brawling, or fighting them, they either choose an extra option or mark 1 XP (their choice). Training Exercise. When you Make Camp, you and your comrade can choose the same Condition together. Until you next Make Camp, you both ignore penalties from that Condition. ☐ Exhausted ☐ Frightened ☐ Angry ☐ Distracted ☐ Insecure
bondTexts.enthusiasts: Shared Interest: (e.g. arena fights, birds, cooking, local politics, magic, secret history) Joy of Discovery. Once per session, when you discover something new related to your Shared Interest, clear a Condition. If your fellow enthusiast is present for the discovery, or when you show/tell them later, choose one from Comfort or Support. Great Minds. When you Spout Lore about your Interest, if your fellow enthusiast could answer “Yes” to a question, then you can too, even if they aren't nearby. ✷On a 12+, your bondmate may answer instead of the GM. Paired Project. When you Enjoy Downtime, you can begin working on a project together related to your Shared Interest. Say what it is, and the GM will give you 1-4 requirements (similar to Perform a Ritual). When you meet the requirements, you finish the project and each mark 1 Depth with each other (in addition to the project's effects). When you Enjoy Downtime with a paired project already underway, together you may ask the GM any one question about it. Specialists. When you Defy Danger in direct relation to your Shared Interest, ignore penalties from Conditions.
bondTexts.student-and-teacher: I am the ☐ Student ☐ Teacher Words of Wisdom. Once per session, when the Teacher gives advice or guidance to the Student, the Teacher says what the Student should do. If the Student accepts, their first roll in pursuit of it has adv. If the Student rejects it, the Teacher marks a Condition but the Student clears one. Either way, if the Student achieves it later, the Student marks 1 XP and the Teacher clears a Condition. Heroic Sacrifice. When the Student Faces Death, the Teacher may take their place, clearing a Condition (and joining the scene if they were absent). When the Teacher dies, they can give the Student a final word of guidance, either here and now or based on their last conversation. From now on, until they see the Teacher again (if ever), when the Student Ends the Session having followed that guidance, they mark 1 XP. Just Like We Practiced. Once per session each, the Teacher and the Student can Aid one another without any cost or risk. The Sincerest Form of Flattery. When the Teacher Senses Motive, they may always ask the Student one additional question, even if they're Sensing another. When the Student imitates a mannerism or ability from the Teacher, the Student may mark a Condition to gain access to one of the Teacher’s Moves for the rest of the scene (Student's call).
bondTexts.rivals: Always a Competition. When you start each session, neither of you has the Upper Hand. When you End the Session, whoever has the Upper Hand marks 1 XP. Between the two of you, only one can have the Upper Hand at a time. When you pull off an impressive feat or dangerous trick, ask your rival if they agree. If they do, gain the Upper Hand. If they don't, either gain adv on your next roll or erase 1 Depth with them to gain the Upper Hand anyways (your call). I Can Do That. When you Aid your rival by copying their actions, instead of giving them adv you may roll at the same time with your own Stat. If your result is higher, they can use it instead and you have the Upper Hand. Still Counts as One. Once per session, when you admit that your rival went above and beyond or did the impossible, they may make one choice from Comfort or Support. Try to Keep Up. When you gain the Upper Hand, you may taunt your rival to clear a Condition. If you do, they get adv to their next roll.
bondTexts.romantic-partners: Always on My Mind. Once per session each, you can wonder dreamily about your lover to gain adv on a roll as if they were Aiding you (at no cost). Handfasting. When you both commit to a lifelong partnership, each of you can now use Always on My Mind a number of times per session equal to your current Depth with your bondmate (min 1). Let Me Tell You All About Them. When you wax poetically about your lover to an NPC, you can Pull Strings+your Depth with your lover (instead of +CHA). Together Forever. When either of you dies, the GM will tell the other how to bring you back to life. At the end of the next session (not this one), if you haven’t revived your lover, you follow them in death.
bondTexts.siblings: Look Out For Each Other. When your sibling is about to mark a Condition or suffer dmg, if it makes sense in the fiction, you can mark the Condition or suffer the dmg instead. I Carry Your Heart with Me. When your sibling dies, they choose one of their Advanced Moves; you can now use it even after you erase this Bond. Push Your Buttons. When you try and convince your sibling to do something they don’t want to, they can clear a Condition if they reluctantly go along—or mark a Condition if they don’t. Shared Past. When you Comfort or Support your sibling, you can also ask “Did we talk about a happy memory we share?”

The new result is what really happens. No Rest for the All-Seeing (-) — When you finish Making Camp successfully, you recover only half the amount of HP you normally would (rounded down).
struggleTexts.pariah: Questions: What aspect about you is reviled? Do you hide your reviled aspect or revel in it? If you, would you get rid of it? Monster! (+) — When you first reveal your reviled aspect to an NPC, they’re surprised for a moment and they’re now #afraid of you . You get adv to Defy Danger, Pull Strings, or Trade Blows against any NPC who’s #afraid of you. Wretch (-) — You get dis to Defy Danger, Pull Strings, or Trade Blows against any NPC who isn’t #afraid of you.
struggleTexts.reformed: Questions: Which PC used to be your enemy? Who doesn’t think you've changed? What do you regret the most? Haunted (+-) — You start with 2 Guilt; mark it now. When you act selfishly, you may mark Guilt to gain adv on a roll. Whenever you have fewer marked+locked Conditions than your Guilt (including when you first gain this Struggle), immediately mark Conditions until they match. Reparation (+) — Once per session, when you significantly help an NPC (GM's call), clear 1 Guilt and a Condition. Retribution (+) — When you Trade Blows with someone from your villainous past, add your Guilt to all dmg dealt to them.
struggleTexts.renowned: Questions: How do the stories depict you? What's the most difficult part to live up to? What other PC is a frequent side character? Rumors & Legends (+-) — Your Fame starts at 1. At the start of each session, tell the group a story someone heard about you. If your Fame is 2 or more, the GM may then add a twist or complication someone else heard. When you End the Session, if you lived up to the story (GM's final say), gain 1 Fame (max 3). Otherwise, lose 1 Fame (min -1) and mark a Condition. Larger Than Life (+) — When you interact with the public, or try to live up to this session's story, you may roll+Fame instead of another stat. If you do, ✷on a 9 or lower, you also reduce your Fame by 1.
struggleTexts.secret-identity: Questions: What’s your real name and appearance? Who are “the wrong people”? What nefarious scheme do they want you for? Scion (+) — Once per session, you can mark one of the following to get temporary access to: ☐ ancient lore ☐ bountiful resources ☐ iconic treasure ☐ powerful allies ☐ unique magic source. When you assume your real identity, clear one of the boxes. Unmasked (-) — When your real identity is revealed to someone new, the GM may have the wrong people get news of you or the GM advances a Threat (GM’s call).
struggleTexts.treasure-obsession: Questions: What is the treasure and what the legends say about it? Why is it so important to you? Who is a dangerous and deadly competitor for it? On the Trail (+) — Once per session, after you Spout Lore or Unearth Secrets, mark a Lead to ask the GM a question about your treasure, such as: who guards it, who could abuse it, or what curse it supposedly places on whoever finds it, just to name a few. When you mark your 5th Lead, you can ask the GM: where exactly can I find my treasure? Dragon-Sickness (-) — You can only Comfort or Support (or receive it) from other PCs who have promised to help you obtain your treasure.
struggleTexts.vengeful: Questions: Who’s your archenemy? What did they take from you? What stands between you and satisfaction? Unwavering (+) — When you Trade Blows with your archenemy (or anyone associated with them), roll dmg with adv. Once per session, while pursuing your archenemy, when you would Face Death, you instead stay at 1 HP. Consumed (-) — When you would take a course of action that pulls you away from vengeance against your archenemy, mark a Condition.

magicItems.name: adamantine armor
magicItems.description: This suit of medium or heavy metallic armor is reinforced with adamantine, one of the hardest substances in existence While you're wearing it, any time you would suffer max dmg, instead they just roll with adv.

magicItems.name: alchemy jug
magicItems.description: A seemingly-ordinary 1 gallon ceramic jug When you speak its magic word, one of the following liquids fills the jug (your call): ✦ acid ✦ basic poison ✦ beer ✦ fresh water ✦ mayonnaise ✦ oil ✦ saltwater ✦ vinegar ✦ wine

magicItems.name: animated rope
magicItems.description: A rope that listens and sometimes wags one of its ends like a tail. Does tricks, too, like a smart and more obedient snake might When you command the rope to perform a simple action (within its capabilities), it does so. Example orders include: ✦ coil ✦ come here ✦ slack

magicItems.name: animated shield
magicItems.description: This shield has been enchanted to follow its owner around and protect them. It’s sometimes overzealous in its duty This shield floats near you, and protects you of its own volition without you needing to hold or wear it. Mark a use to ignore all dmg from one attack.

magicItems.name: armor of vulnerability
magicItems.description: #cursed This golden suit of armor never needs to be polished Choose one type of dmg from the following: divine, magical, or physical. While you're wearing it, you suffer only half the dmg of the chosen type. Cursed. You cannot take this armor off unless you find a way to lift its curse. While you're wearing it, you suffer double the dmg of any type not chosen above.

magicItems.name: arrow of slaying
magicItems.description: This arrow is a magic weapon meant to slay a specific kind of creature Examples include: angel, demon, devil, dragon, or giant, just to name a few. Against such a creature the arrow has #piercing and, ✷on a 12+ when you Trade Blows, it kills the creature immediately and the arrow’s magic is gone.

magicItems.name: arrows of acheron
magicItems.description: Crafted in darkness by a blind fletcher, these arrows disintegrate if ever touched by the light of the sun Mark a use to have your arrows ignore all darkness, blindness, and concealment for a scene.

magicItems.name: bag of holding
magicItems.description: This ordinary-looking belt pouch that smells faintly of ozone This bag can contain a cart’s worth of volume and weight, while still weighing and measuring as if it was empty.

magicItems.name: barb of the Black Gate
magicItems.description: A nail or spike, twisted and forever cold, said to have been pried from the Gates of Death themselves When you embed the barb into a corpse, it disappears and ensures that corpse will never be risen again—no one and nothing but Death himself can reignite the flame of life (or unlife) in the body.

magicItems.name: bead of force
magicItems.description: This small black sphere measures 3/4 of an inch in diameter and weighs an ounce Typically, 1d4+4 beads of force are found together. You can throw it up to #near and the bead explodes on impact (and is destroyed). Everyone within #close of the explosion is trapped inside a sphere of transparent force that fills the area until the end of the scene. The sphere can be picked up, and its magic causes it to weigh only 1 pound, regardless of the weight of creatures inside.

magicItems.name: berserker axe
magicItems.description: #cursed This giant, double-headed axe has a bloodstain that always look fresh—and can’t be rubbed away While you wield this axe, you get +1 to your dmg rolls and your max HP increases by your STR (min 1). Cursed. You cannot wield any other weapon or let go of the axe unless you find a way to lift its curse. While you're wielding it, any time you deal dmg you or one of your allies (your call) suffers the same amount.

magicItems.name: dancing sword
magicItems.description: A long thin blade that emits a faint humming tune, even while sheathed When you toss the sword into the air it begins to sing, flies around within #near range, and attacks your foes until the end of the scene. If it fights alone, it deals 1d6 dmg and becomes Helpless if attacked. If you fight alongside it, add 1d6 to your dmg.

magicItems.name: dust of disappearance
magicItems.description: Found in a small packet, this powder resembles very fine sand When you throw the dust into the air, you and each creature and object within #close of you become invisible until the end of the scene. If someone under the effect of the dust Trades Blows or Casts a Spell, the invisibility ends for them.

magicItems.name: dust of dryness
magicItems.description: This magical sand contains a mote from the earth dimension This small packet contains 1d6+4 pinches of dust. When you sprinkle a pinch over a cube of water it transforms into one marble-sized pellet. The pellet's weight is negligible. You can smash the pellet against a hard surface, causing the pellet to shatter and the water to be released. When you expose a creature mostly composed of water to a pinch of dust, you need to Trade Blows+DEX. ✷On a 12+, the creature’s destroyed. ✷On a 10+, you inflict 2d6 dmg #piercing on them. ✷On a 7-9, you inflict only 1d6 dmg #piercing.

magicItems.name: dust of sneezing and choking
magicItems.description: #cursed This powder appears to be dust of disappearance When you throw the dust into the air, you and each creature and object within #close of you that needs to breathe become unable to do so while sneezing uncontrollably. You roll+DEX for everyone involved. ✷On a 10+, everyone escapes quickly, each suffering only 1d6 dmg #piercing. ✷On a 7-9, the escape takes longer, so everyone suffers 2d6 dmg #piercing. ✷On a 6-, everyone is at 1 HP and you all become unconscious; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move.

magicItems.name: earworm wax
magicItems.description: A yellowish candle, it seemingly never burns out and its light is strange and weak. Its wax is always cool, too When you drip the wax into someone’s ear, mark 1 Wax to ask your target a question and force them answer with the whole truth, despite themselves.

magicItems.name: efficient quiver
magicItems.description: The quiver connects to an extradimensional space that allows it to hold numerous items while never weighing more than 2 pounds While wearing the efficient quiver, any weapon with #ammo loses the tag.

magicItems.name: elemental gem
magicItems.description: #consumable This gem contains a mote of trapped, vibrant elemental energy When you break the gem, an elemental is summoned from their home dimension and the gem's magic is lost. The type of gem determines the elemental summoned: blue sapphire — air elemental emerald — water elemental red corundum — fire elemental yellow diamond — earth elemental

magicItems.name: eversmoking bottle
magicItems.description: Smoke leaks from the lead-stoppered mouth of this brass bottle, which weighs 1 pound When you remove the stopper, a cloud of thick smoke pours out in a #near area from the bottle. The cloud's area is heavily obscured. As long as the bottle remains open and within the cloud, the area increases until it covers up to #far. The cloud persists as long as the bottle is open. Closing the bottle requires someone speaking a command word. Once the bottle is closed, the cloud disperses.

magicItems.name: forget-me-naught
magicItems.description: This highly secretive and illegal smoky liquid is magically synthesized rather than harvested When you or another ingests forget-me-naught and focuses on a specific memory, you/they forget it forever.

magicItems.name: helm of comprehending languages
magicItems.description: This shiny helm is inscribed with all manner of hieroglyphs, letters, and runes While wearing this helm you can mark a Condition to understand the literal meaning of any spoken language that you hear until the end of the scene. You also understand any written language that you see, but you must be touching the surface on which the words are written.

magicItems.name: horn of blasting
magicItems.description: This silver horn bears the enchantment of the thunder rune When you speak a command word and blow the horn, mark a Condition to have it emit a thunderous blast. Then, roll+CHA. ✷On a 10+, all your enemies #near suffer 1d6 dmg #piercing and are deafened until the end of the scene, and all your allies clear a Condition. ✷On a 7-9, choose one or the other. ✷On a 6-, you get both but the horn explodes, causing you to suffer the same dmg as your enemies and losing all its magic permanently; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move.

magicItems.name: immovable rod
magicItems.description: A funny metal rod with a small button on it When you press the rod’s button, it freezes in place—in midair, standing up or lying down. It can’t be moved. Pull it, push it, try as hard as you like, the rod stays. Maybe it can be destroyed, maybe it can’t. Push the button again and it’s free to move once more.

magicItems.name: magic wand
magicItems.description: Wizards and politicians have spent generations debating the risks and benefits of anyone being able to use magic with these A wand acts like a spell scroll (minor) but isn’t consumed when used. When you first receive the wand, you learn which spell it can cast. When you unleash the magic within the wand, choose one: The wand drains itself, and can’t be used again until you next successfully Make Camp The wand drains you; mark a Condition

magicItems.name: marvelous pigments
magicItems.description: Typically found in 1d4 pots inside a fine wooden box with a brush (weighing 1 pound in total) These pigments allow you to create three-dimensional objects by painting them in two dimensions. When you complete the painting, mark 1 use and the object or terrain feature depicted becomes a permanent, nonmagical part of reality.

magicItems.name: mithral armor
magicItems.description: This suit of medium or heavy metallic armor is made of mithral, a light and flexible metal A mithral chain shirt or breastplate can be worn under normal clothes. Any mithral armor has no STR requirement to be used properly.

magicItems.name: oil of slipperiness
magicItems.description: This sticky black unguent is thick and heavy in the container, but it flows quickly when poured Mark the use to cover someone of human size or smaller (along with the equipment they’re wearing and carrying). Until they Make Camp, the target cannot be slowed down, paralyzed, or restrained. Alternatively, the oil can be poured on the ground, covering up to #close. Anyone inside this area—or who enters it—falls prone. This effect lasts until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: philter of love
magicItems.description: This philter's rose-hued, effervescent liquid contains one easy-to-miss bubble shaped like a heart When someone drinks this philter, the next time the imbiber sees someone they become charmed until the end of the scene. If the imbiber’s alloromantic, they regard that person as their true love while this effect lasts.

magicItems.name: phylactery
magicItems.description: You've bound your soul to a #hidden #warded vessel and escaped the grasp of true death. Special: This magic item can only be gained through Shed This Mortal Coil from the Wizard's Necromancer Path. While your phylactery is intact, gain the following: After you die, you return from death in a newly reformed body, and rejoin your allies the next time they Make Camp. You still lock a Condition from Facing Death. When you Cast a Spell using both a substance and a verb from the Necromancy School, treat the mag as if it were 1 lower when comparing it to your Casting Stat If your Phylactery is ever destroyed, you can spend (8 - Necromancer Moves gained) Treasure to create a new one when you Enjoy Downtime.

magicItems.name: portable hole
magicItems.description: A silky black cloth, folded like a handkerchief, that can unfold to 6 feet across When you spread the full cloth across a surface, such as a wall or floor, it becomes a 10ft deep extradimensional pit. Fold it up again, and anyone or anything inside is trapped if they don’t escape in time.

magicItems.name: potion of animal friendship
magicItems.description: Agitating this muddy liquid brings little bits into view: a fish scale, a hummingbird tongue, a cat claw, or a squirrel hair When you drink this potion, you can charm one beast you can see until the end of the scene. While charmed, the beast will try to fulfill your commands to the best of their ability.

magicItems.name: potion of clairvoyance
magicItems.description: An eyeball bobs in this yellowish liquid, but vanishes when the potion is opened When you drink this potion, you choose seeing or hearing. Until the end of the scene, you can either see or hear in a location you’re familiar with or in an obvious location unfamiliar to you until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: potion of climbing
magicItems.description: The potion is separated into brown, silver, and gray layers resembling bands of stone When you drink this potion, you can climb any surface at the same speed you usually walk until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: potion of diminution
magicItems.description: The red in the potion's liquid continuously contracts to a tiny bead and then expands to color the clear liquid around it When you drink this potion, your size is halved in all dimensions, and your weight is reduced to one-eighth of normal until you next Make Camp. You get adv to Sneak Past while this effect lasts. Everything you’re wearing and carrying changes size with you, and returns to normal when you drop it.

magicItems.name: potion of flying
magicItems.description: This potion's clear liquid floats at the top of its container and has cloudy white impurities drifting in it When you drink this potion, you can fly and hover at the same speed you usually walk until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: potion of gaseous form
magicItems.description: This potion's container seems to hold fog that moves and pours like water When you drink this potion, you and everything you’re wearing and carrying transforms into an #incorporeal misty cloud until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: potion of growth
magicItems.description: The red in the potion's liquid continuously contracts to a tiny bead and then expands to color the clear liquid around it When you drink this potion, your size doubles in all dimensions, and your weight is multiplied by 8 until you next Make Camp. You inflict +1d4 dmg while this effect lasts. Everything you’re wearing and carrying changes size with you, and returns to normal when you drop it.

magicItems.name: potion of healing
magicItems.description: The potion's red liquid glimmers when agitated When you drink this potion, recover half your lost HP (rounded down) or clear one locked Condition.

magicItems.name: potion of heroism
magicItems.description: This blue potion bubbles and steams as if boiling When you drink this potion, you get +1d4 to your next Move roll and to your next dmg roll. Also, the next time you Face Death, if you choose to Gamble with Death, you get adv.

magicItems.name: potion of invisibility
magicItems.description: This potion's container looks empty but feels as though it holds liquid When you drink this potion, you become invisible until you Cast a Spell, inflict dmg, Trade Blows, or the scene ends. Anything you wear or carry is invisible with you.

magicItems.name: potion of poison
magicItems.description: #cursed This concoction looks, smells, and tastes like a potion of healing or other beneficial potion When you drink this potion, roll+STR. ✷On a 10+, you were able to withstand most of the poison’s effect; suffer only 1d6 dmg #piercing.✷On a 7-9, you suffer 2d6 dmg #piercing and are #poisoned (dis to all rolls until you stop being poisoned). ✷On a 6-, you need to Face Death; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move.

magicItems.name: potion of resistance
magicItems.description: The color of this dense liquid varies depending on the type When you drink this potion, any dmg rolls of the chosen type get dis against you until the end of the scene. The types (and potion colors) include: acid (caustic green) fire (molten red) holy (golden yellow) lighting (electric blue) magic (jade black) poison (mud green) psychic (wild rose) unholy (crimson red)

magicItems.name: potion of speed
magicItems.description: The potion's yellow fluid is streaked with black and swirls on its own When you drink this potion, you can move twice as quickly, you get +1 to your armor and adv to any DEX-based rolls until the scene ends. When the effect ends, mark Exhausted.

magicItems.name: potion of water breathing
magicItems.description: Its cloudy green fluid smells of the sea and has a jellyfish-like bubble floating in it When you drink this potion, you can breathe underwater until the end of the scene.

magicItems.name: restorative ointment
magicItems.description: This glass jar, 3 inches in diameter, contains 1d4+1 doses of a thick mixture that smells faintly of aloe. The jar and its contents weigh 1/2 pound When you apply to the skin or swallow a dose, you recover 1d8 HP, stop being #poisoned, and are cure of any disease.

magicItems.name: ring of warmth
magicItems.description: Three miniature white arctic foxes curled together on the outer side of a ring lined with fluffy white fur on the inside While wearing this ring you don’t mark Conditions or suffer dmg from extremely cold environments. In addition, everything you wear and carry are unharmed by low temperatures.

magicItems.name: sending stones
magicItems.description: Two identical marbles with matching symbols carved into them When you speak into one stone, the other emits your voice.

magicItems.name: sovereign glue
magicItems.description: This viscous, milky-white substance can form a permanent adhesive bond between any two objects When found, a container has 1d6+1 uses left. One use can cover a 1-foot square surface and it takes 1 minute to set. Once it has done so, the bond it creates can only be broken by the application of universal solvent or oil of etherealness.

magicItems.name: spell scroll (minor)
magicItems.description: An ancient-looking parchment scroll sealed with a pale-white ribbon and a golden wax seal impressed with an unknown symbol When you read this scroll, its magic is consumed and you can Cast a Spell+INT with an effect of mag 0 or 1. The spell scroll is considered a magic item you can use and ✷on a 7-9, it doesn’t grant you a unique option.

magicItems.name: staff of the adder
magicItems.description: A wood staff carved into the face of a snake When you wield and command this staff, it transforms into a venomous snake which understands and follows your commands until the end of the scene. Venomous Snake — 3 HP, 1 Armor (bark-like skin), 1d4 dmg (bite). Poison. PCs bitten must roll+STR. ✷On a 7-9, they suffer 1d4 extra poison dmg. ✷On a 6-, they suffer 2d4 extra poison dmg

magicItems.name: sword of life stealing
magicItems.description: This blade’s crossguard and pommel are ornate, decorated with skull motifs. The grip is wrapped in black material with red accents and tied with red ribbons While you wield this sword when you Trade Blows, ✷on a 12+, you inflict +1d6 dmg as long as your opponent isn’t a construct or undead, and you regain HP equal to the total dmg you inflicted.

magicItems.name: tears of Annalise
magicItems.description: Cloudy red gemstones the size of a thumbnail, the tears of Annalise are always found in pairs When you and another PC each swallow a tear, you can feel the other’s strong emotions, particularly sadness, loss, fear, or desire. Whenever one of you marks a Condition, the other may mark one instead. The effects last until one spills the blood of the other.

magicItems.name: trident of fish command
magicItems.description: This trident has a staff made of dark, weathered wood, adorned with rough, organic textures and sharp, dark green barnacle-like growths near the base While you wield this trident, you can mark a use and roll+WIS to telepathically connect with a beast native to water. ✷On a 10+, you take total control of the creature’s actions until the end of the scene. ✷On a 7-9, you can give the creature a single, simple command that they’ll follow to the best of their ability. ✷On a 6-, the creature sees you as a menace; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move.

magicItems.name: universal solvent
magicItems.description: This tube holds milky liquid with a strong alcohol smell When you mark a use and pour the contents of the tube onto a surface within reach, the liquid instantly dissolves up to 1 square foot of adhesive it touches, including sovereign glue.

magicItems.name: vicious weapon
magicItems.description: A weapon with an ornate gold basket hilt and a long, thin steel blade While you wield this weapon when you Trade Blows, ✷on a 12+, you inflict +1d6 dmg.

magicItems.name: Alveric’s Soulstealer Blade
magicItems.description: This obsidian, rune-engraved weapon is rumored to be more than a mere instrument of destruction Devourer of Souls. When you take a person's life with Soulstealer, it absorbs their soul; mark a box in the Trapped Souls track above. When you mark the fifth box, clear the track and unlock one of the Moves below. While wielding it, you can replace your STR stat with the number of Soulstealer Moves you have unlocked (min. +1, max. +4). Gravity-Defying Menace. Clear one Trapped Soul to have Soulstealer fight on its own or fly to your hand from afar. Reality Rifter. When you use Soulstealer to open a rift in reality, connecting the world you’re currently in with another you know of, treat it as Perform a Ritual with the blade as the font of magical power. After the GM tells you the requirements you may clear Trapped Souls, 1-for-1, to profanely fulfill them. The Great Banisher. When you Trade Blows while wielding Soulstealer, and your opponent is a Bloodied outsider, ✷On a 10+, you can banish them from the Material world permanently. Mark a box in the Trapped Souls track. They cannot manifest again until you die or that box is cleared.

unlocks.name: Gravity-Defying Menace
unlocks.text: Gravity-Defying Menace. Clear one Trapped Soul to have Soulstealer fight on its own or fly to your hand from afar.

unlocks.name: Reality Rifter
unlocks.text: Reality Rifter. When you use Soulstealer to open a rift in reality, connecting the world you’re currently in with another you know of, treat it as Perform a Ritual with the blade as the font of magical power. After the GM tells you the requirements you may clear Trapped Souls, 1-for-1, to profanely fulfill them.

unlocks.name: The Great Banisher
unlocks.text: The Great Banisher. When you Trade Blows while wielding Soulstealer, and your opponent is a Bloodied outsider, ✷On a 10+, you can banish them from the Material world permanently. Mark a box in the Trapped Souls track. They cannot manifest again until you die or that box is cleared.

magicItems.name: Caliburnus, The Sword That Heals
magicItems.description: A legendary sword that can only wielded by those the weapon deems worthy Rightful Touch. When you touch someone you deem worthy with Caliburnus’ flat side, mark Ruin so they recover Xd6 HP, where X equals your CHA. When you mark the fifth box, clear the track and unlock one of the Moves below. Caliburnus is virtually indestructible. While wielding it, you can replace your CHA stat with the number of Caliburnus Moves you have available (min +1, max +4) A New Dawn. When you raise Caliburnus towards the sky and cry out for light, the blade lights up with the radiance of thirty torches; mark Ruin and roll+CHA. ✷On a 10+, choose two from below. ✷On a 7-9, only one. The shining light illuminates a secret, treasure, or opportunity You and all your allies up to #far clear a Condition Each evildoer up to #far suffers 1d6 #holy #piercing dmg ✷On a 6-, the light draws the ire of evil forces; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move. Bright Eyes. You may mark Ruin to see through any concealment, deception, or illusion, as well as feel the presence of magic all around you. Promised Victory. When you would Face Death, you can mark Ruin equal to your CHA and remain at 1 HP instead. If you ever reach 5 Ruin and have no further Moves to take, your ruin has finally come. Your character must leave the Material world and Caliburnus must be returned to its keeper.

unlocks.name: A New Dawn
unlocks.text: A New Dawn. When you raise Caliburnus towards the sky and cry out for light, the blade lights up with the radiance of thirty torches; mark Ruin and roll+CHA. ✷On a 10+, choose two from below. ✷On a 7-9, only one. The shining light illuminates a secret, treasure, or opportunity You and all your allies up to #far clear a Condition Each evildoer up to #far suffers 1d6 #holy #piercing dmg ✷On a 6-, the light draws the ire of evil forces; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move.

unlocks.name: Bright Eyes
unlocks.text: Bright Eyes. You may mark Ruin to see through any concealment, deception, or illusion, as well as feel the presence of magic all around you.

unlocks.name: Promised Victory
unlocks.text: Promised Victory. When you would Face Death, you can mark Ruin equal to your CHA and remain at 1 HP instead. If you ever reach 5 Ruin and have no further Moves to take, your ruin has finally come. Your character must leave the Material world and Caliburnus must be returned to its keeper.

magicItems.name: Elleovene’s Circlet of Supreme Mesmerism
magicItems.description: An apparently simple silver circlet with a blue jewel at its center Awakened Mind. You can read sapient beings’ superficial thoughts and you can focus on someone #near to delve into their deeper mind. For the purposes of Sensing Motive of someone #near, this focus counts as intimate or prying conversation. You no longer mark Conditions. When instructed to do so, you can either mark Stone Heart above or lock a Condition. When you mark the fifth Stone Heart box, clear the track and unlock one of the Moves below. Master of Puppets. When you touch someone skin-to-skin and force your mind on them, roll+WIS. ✷On a 7+, choose one below. ✷On a 7-9, mark Stone Heart due to the effort. They answer two of your questions as if you Sensed their Motive They follow a simple command until the scene ends They forget a memory ✷On a 6-, mark 1 XP and they choose one for you instead. Spy the World’s Mind Web. When you expand your mind to sense all of the Material world’s mind, roll+WIS. ✷On a 7+, the GM will tell you one detail of a Threat (Asset, Development, or Reaction). ✷On a 7-9, you also choose one below: Somebody unwelcome knows of your spying You suffer from psychic whiplash; mark 2 Stone Heart boxes ✷On a 6-, something or someone’s blocking you; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move. Willbreaker. When you unleash your mind's power upon someone #near, roll+WIS. ✷On a 10+, choose two from below. ✷On a 7-9, only one. They can’t act until they’re harmed or the scene ends They suffer 1d10 #piercing dmg from mental overload You can use this again this scene (otherwise you can’t) ✷On a 6-, they were somehow ready for you; mark 1 XP and the GM makes a Move. If you would ever mark the fifth box and you have no further Moves to take, you lose your character, as you become an NPC that’s transcended the mortal condition.

unlocks.name: Master of Puppets

content.text: These are the core overarching goals you have while running a game of Dungeon World 2. Even if you forget or miss other parts of this chapter, the Agenda is what you should refer to when in need of guidance. Your Agenda every session is:
Fill the Player Characters' lives with adventure
Play to find out what happens
Portray a meaningful fantasy world
Fill the Player Characters' lives with adventure

By “life of adventure” we mean one of highs and lows, victories and defeats, drinks with friends, hard roads, swollen bruises, and open laughter. Give the PCs opportunities (and motives) to accomplish exciting things, but don't make it too easy (or it won’t be adventurous). We recommend you put the Player Characters in situations that test them, hurt them, exploit their weaknesses, show off their strengths, and/or tempt their desires… Then see how they handle it all. We encourage you to celebrate their successes, mourn their losses, and anticipate—as best as you can—what they might do next.
You may need to prepare (or “prep” in TTRPG parlance) the ingredients of an adventure ahead of time, such as:
ideas for Potential Scenes
details (and stats when necessary) for Important NPCs & Villains
descriptions for some Fantastic Locations and, of course,
some Rewards.
If you want more guidance about how to Prep a Session, check here.
If you prefer to improvise, at least knowing that these ingredients are important to create an adventure should help you with coming up with them in the moment.
Play to Find Out What Happens

The key difference between a TTRPG and any other type of game or fiction is that in these games—and DW2 is no different—no one knows what will happen in advance. You as the GM may do some setup, but the Players and their PCs will interact with your preparation and change the situation, often in ways you can't predict. On the flip side, every time the PCs attempt something, they’re confronted with the fictional world that you portray and its often unexpected (especially to them) consequences.

This back and forth creates a wonderful unknown that is discovered, through play, by the whole table together. This is what we mean with play to find out what happens! We invite you to embrace this uncertainty, and to empower the Players to do the same. So, don't hold on to your prep or ideas too hard, because they'll probably never come true in exactly the way you imagined them. Similarly, Players shouldn't really grow too attached to their plans or even their PCs, because something could always happen that changes everything.
Portray a Meaningful Fantasy World

Fantasy fiction and games—and DW2 is no different—include many elements that do not and could never exist in our world, such as magic, nonhuman sapient beings, and other dimensions that can’t usually be accessed physically, among many others. “Fantasy” may seem like an obvious concept these days, but such worlds have become so filled with mundanity as to not feel truly fantastical anymore.

We believe that what makes fantasy worlds amazing is the right mixture of wonder and believability. If you focus on wonder too much, the world (and game) often feels inconsistent and driven by whim, which can reduce the emotional impact of events and consequences. On the other hand, focusing purely on believability will make the world feel predictable, sterile, or boring— too close to what we are already familiar with. As such, we recommend you don't try to rationalize or unnecessarily justify the fantastical elements in the world, and instead leave room for new and peculiar forms of the impossible to appear later.

The abstract ideal lies in a balance between the two. The specific proportions will depend on you and your group’s preferences, so you’ll probably need to discuss this with them during Session Zero procedures, but here are some ideas for adding both to your world.
To make your world more wondrous:
Incorporate unique aspects of your world into its factions, traditions, and civilizations
Introduce something unique and magical, such as a location, creature, or phenomenon
Make the world’s environments vibrant, with dangerous inhabitants and colorful flora and fauna
To make your world feel more believable:
Describe what the PCs see and hear, yes, but also what they smell, touch, and more. How warm is the fire? What does the room smell like after a magical lightning is unleashed within it?
Give its inhabitants human emotions and struggles. Maybe elves don't sleep or age, but they still struggle with love, loss, and fear, even if they might express it in unusual ways.

Show how the passage of time affects people and places. This could be as simple as a holiday festival, or a change in leadership, an ongoing project, or a collapsing building. Change, growth, and decay all overlap
If the Agenda are your objectives/goals as a GM, then the Principles are your ways/roads of getting there, your specific guidelines on how to achieve them. In short, they are:
Be a fan of the Players & their characters
Describe with dramatic detail
Give every NPC a motivation
Let the Players roleplay with each other
Use the PCs’ names whenever possible
Be a Fan of the Players and Their Characters

While authentically portraying the world (and its consequences) may lead you to harm the PCs, you are neither an “antagonistic enemy” to them nor an “impartial referee” of their actions. We envision you, the GM, as someone who’s purposefully on the side of the PCs, collaborating with the Players to go on adventures and have fun at the table.

Going even beyond that, we recommend that you try and be a fan of the Players at your table. This should lead you, hopefully, to create a cooperative environment in which everyone feels comfortable speaking up, offering their own ideas, and being creative. We dearly encourage you to incorporate the Players’ ideas into the game as much as you can, even if they seem weird or discordant at first. In short: try to “Yes, and…” as much as possible, and reserve your “No”s to the moments when you really need them.
Describe with Dramatic Detail

When describing characters, environments, and actions, we invite you to aim for vivid, dynamic language. A yeti doesn’t just swing its claws—it roars, grabs its victim, and drags them towards their frozen lair. A burning acid swamp doesn't just bubble corrosively; the air burns your nostrils as clouds of colorful insects bite you.

It takes practice to become good at this, but often the best way to start is to focus on a few specific details and let the Players’ imaginations fill in the rest. If you describe a brilliant apothecary with thick glasses, a simmering scowl, swarmed by a dozen scrambling assistants, then that’s more than enough to convey a strong impression of her.

In contrast, we think that the best way to communicate larger scale situations is in down-to-earth ways. If there is a plague sweeping through a city, then maybe evoke the feeling of decaying streets, describe the smell of burning bodies, and have a coughing beggar ask for change.
Give every NPC a motivation

Non-player characters (NPCs) are your characters in the game. As such, the best advice we can offer on how to portray them better is to know why they do what they do. In writing, this is often referred to as a character’s motivation, desire, or goal. We use the term Drive in our NPC statblocks. The idea is the same: knowing a character’s underlying reason for acting the way they do will make it easier for you to roleplay them.  Additionally, if the PCs come to learn that reason, it will add a sense of believability to the fantasy world you’re all building together.
Let the Players roleplay with each other

One of the most common foibles among GMs is that we just speak too much. We want to “fill the silence,” so to speak, to keep things moving, and to make the whole game as entertaining as possible for everyone involved. The “problem” is that part of the fun of playing a TTRPG is roleplaying PC-PC interactions when you are a Player. DW2, even more so, has as a core part of its vision the idea that PCs are encouraged to form deep Bonds with each other. And even though that may happen mechanically without that much actual roleplay, the ideal is that the Players feel that their characters are getting closer to one another in the fiction.

So, in short: every once in a while just shut up, sit back, and enjoy your Players roleplaying with each other. Let it happen naturally, and don’t intervene unless you’re required to. The adventure will be ready when they are.
Use the PCs’ names whenever possible

If you’re running the game for people you know, it may feel weird or awkward to refer to them by invented fantasy names. As true as that may be, though, if you talk to them by using their real names, you’re referring to them as Players outside of the fiction, and that isn’t a good way to encourage them to roleplay their PCs. Instead, learn by heart and use the PCs’ names as much as you can, so Players are subtly pushed to answer questions and look at things in the fiction from their PC’s perspective which may, in some cases, greatly differ from their own.

These Moves are the way in which you as the GM add to the conversation, altering the fiction directly. This is one of the ways in which the role of GM differs from that of a Player: the Players need to trigger Moves (and usually roll dice) to alter the fiction, while you just get to make a Move, either when instructed or when you think it’s appropriate.
When to Make a GM Move
Generally you should make a GM Move when…
A Player rolls a 6- on a Move
The Players look to you for a response or answer
You have a golden opportunity
A Player rolls a 6- on a Move

This one’s easy. All Moves in the game that include dice-rolling on the part of the Players—and thus can produce a 6- result—will tell you on the Move’s text that you get to make a GM Move as a result. Which GM Move will depend on the specific situation, but the most important decision is whether the Move will be “hard” or “soft” (see Hard & Soft Moves for more info).
The Players look to you for a response or answer

This one is often automatic. The Players want to know what will happen next, and they look at you to portray the world to them. How does the sleeping troll react to the spell's magic? What's behind the secret door they just opened? Make a GM Move and describe what happens in response to their actions.
Sometimes a moment may be tense enough that you might think dice should be rolled. Check if any available PC Moves apply, but if none do then the tension is yours to resolve with a GM Move.
You have a golden opportunity

If the players do something that is an exceptionally bad (or good) idea, they're giving you a golden opportunity to make an appropriate GM Move, even if you interrupt them or override something. For example, if a PC swings their weapon by jumping into a dragon's open mouth, then maybe instead of triggering Trade Blows they just take damage or are outright swallowed. On the other hand, if they offer an NPC the very jewel they've been secretly longing for, then maybe they don't need to Pull Strings, as the NPC may just agree to their offer.
Hard & Soft Moves
A GM Move can be described as “hard” or “soft” based on the severity of its consequences, and how much the PCs can do to negate or recover from it.
Hard Moves

A hard Move is when something changes in the fiction in a way that can’t easily be undone, such as an ally getting seriously wounded, a treasure getting lost or stolen, or an enemy escaping the PC’s grasp. Hard Moves are typically described with the full consequences, with the PCs only being asked “What do you do?” after this happens, rather than before or during the resolution of the Move.

For example: “The elementalist raises a crackling orb high in one hand, and even as you dive for her, a bolt of lightning arcs straight into the market center, detonating several barrels in a fiery explosion”.  In this case, the unrecoverable consequence here is the explosion.
Soft Moves

On the other hand, a soft Move lets the PCs intervene before the consequences are fully in effect. Maybe you describe a sword swinging towards a PC, but they still have a chance to dodge or block it, or you ominously hint at strange lights coming from the sealed tower in the center of town, giving the PCs a chance to investigate. Soft Moves are often used to warn the PCs of future Hard Moves, sometimes imminent ones and sometimes distant.

For example: “The duchess pauses her speech to look at each face in the crowd. You suppress goosebumps as her gaze meets yours, before moving on to the next guest. It seems she’s heard rumors of your plan.” The soft Move here is that the PCs may be under suspicion.
GM Core Moves

Other Powered by the Apocalypse (PbtA) games present sets of GM Moves that are highly evocative and specific, describing as many Moves available to the GM as possible. In DW2 we’ve decided for a more didactic approach, if you will. We assume you’ve never run another PbtA before and, as such, our list of GM Moves is less extensive and more general, trying to point to the most fundamental actions a GM can take in more or less broad strokes.

To make the GM Moves as easy to remember and apply while running the game, we’ve further divided them into three main categories: GM Moves that increase the tension; GM Moves that release the tension; and GM Moves that ask for a Player’s input.
Within these three subdivisions, the specific GM Core Moves are:
Increase the tension
Have one or more PCs pay a cost
Make the situation worse
Skip to the middle of the action
Release the tension
Allow for a moment of respite
Make the situation better
Ask for a Player’s input
Ask someone to describe something
Present the PCs with a decision
Here are the GM Core Moves described in detail.
Allow for a moment of respite

Especially after a moment of high tension—such as a protracted fight or intense negotiation/intrigue Scene—the Players will be looking forward to a moment to relax, Comfort or Support each other, Make Camp, or just talk to each other. It’s very important to grant them these moments because, otherwise, it may feel like too much.
Ask someone to describe something

The most important aspect of a TTRPG is that it is a collaborative effort. If you as the GM are the only one describing the fantasy world, then it becomes your (singular) world instead of your (plural) world. As a result, we advise you to ask the Players—especially those who are on the quieter side—to describe what they’re seeing, to add elements to a location, or to describe a specific quirk of an NPC. With some Players this may feel like pulling teeth at first but, with practice and patience, most Players in our experience end up enjoying these moments of creative spotlight greatly.
Have one or more PCs pay a cost

This can mean to have them mark a use of a piece of equipment, a Condition, or even to lose some precious HP. The important thing here is that PC(s) feel that the situation is getting more dangerous and difficult, so the specific cost will be highly dependent on whatever makes sense in the fiction at the time.
Make the situation better

If every twist in the fiction is bad, then they’ll stop being twists at all, and they’ll become predictable and, worst of all, boring. As such, nice twists are not only desirable but fundamental for good pacing. Having a villain surrender, an unexpected ally appear to help save the day, or just receiving good news can improve the mood of the Players for the better—and restore the enthusiasm after losing badly.
Make the situation worse

Tension increases when things turn from good to bad—or bad to worse—suddenly and unexpectedly, so that the shift in the fiction makes the PCs (and maybe even Players) pay more attention to what’s happening. An ally revealing a betrayal, a wound that turns out to be fatal, or a portcullis that suddenly separates the group are all good examples of this.
Present the PCs with a decision

If you want a situation to feel significant and important to the Players, explain what’s going on and offer them a decision. The more meaningful and difficult the decision, the more the Players will talk about it, invest time and energy, and the more involved they’ll be in seeing through whatever decision/plan of action they invest in.
Skip to the middle of the action

The temptation to describe everything in extreme detail is always there… And we recommend you resist it as much as possible, especially if things are relaxing and you want to increase the tension back up again. Putting the NPCs in an unexpectedly tense but believable situation, out of nowhere, will surely have the PCs jump to action.

During prep, it’s best to outline those NPCs most critical to the Session, focusing on a name and a connection to the fiction, and stating them if necessary. Many other NPC —maybe even most of them—can be improvised right at the table.
Detail Fantastic Locations

In our experience, building evocative locations isn't easily improvised. As such, it's worth spending time writing out a handful of fantastic locations that the characters might discover and explore during the game. Each location can be thought of as a set, a room, or a backdrop for a single Scene in the Session.

Describe each location with a short evocative title such as “The Lost Citadel”. Then write down three descriptors for it, such as: odor of stagnation and slow decay; stone as old as the mountains; strange echoes of sorrow and misery.

Ultimately, whole dungeons can be built from a series of connected fantastic locations, with each location representing a large area or chamber. A specific location might not come up during the game for which you prepare it, but it will be ready for a later session as the PCs explore. Example locations include:
Starting Locations
Often a small settlement from which the PCs set out to explore neighboring lands. A village always works well as a starting location, but there are many alternatives.
Adventurers' guild
Crumbling fortress
Fortress under siege

Great library
Holy temple
Mining outpost

Refugee camp

Ancient crypt
Dangerous caves

Festering well
Faërie glade

Write Down Some Secrets & Clues

Secrets and clues are single short sentences that describe a clue, a piece of the story, or a piece of the world that the characters can discover during the game. You shouldn’t have a fixed idea on how the characters will discover these clues. As such, you'll want to keep these secrets and clues abstract from their place of discovery, so that you can drop them into the game wherever it makes sense. This lets the game flow freely, while still allowing you to reveal important pieces of the story at any point where the characters might discover them. During this step, you might write down ten such secrets or clues. Example secrets and clues include:
Historical Secrets

Use historical secrets to give the PCs meaningful and useful information as they explore the fantasy world. Secrets of this kind should provide characters and Players alike with bite-sized pieces of local or world history.
Historical secrets might be found as mosaics in ancient tombs, statues in old ruins, dusty tomes in ancient libraries, markings on strange weapons, or tales shared among elderly villagers.
What alien creature or power is hidden here?
What ancient civilization once thrived here?
What armies once battled here?
What cruel lord was slain in this place?
What dead god has a connection to the area?
What horrific monster once ruled here?
What old empire's settlements lie buried here?
What primeval mysteries lay buried here?
What rebellion took place here?
What was this location's former purpose?
NPC Secrets
Use NPC secrets to reveal information about these NPCs to the PCs, especially as a means of introducing villains before they face them.
PCs might learn NPC secrets from a herald or sidekick, rumors at a local pub, recovered journals, a minion's last words, captured letters, or town gossip.
What dark history follows the NPC?
What does the NPC desire?
What foe did the NPC defeat?
What great power does the NPC possess?
What makes the NPC politically untouchable?
What makes the NPC think they're right?
What regular routines does the NPC follow?
What secret does the NPC want to keep hidden?
What was the NPC's great accomplishment?
Who does the NPC love above all others?
Player Character Secrets
Use PCs secrets to tie them to the fantasy world. These sorts of secrets might be revealed by NPCs, old journals or letters, suddenly recalled memories, or prophetic dreams.
How is the villain related to the character?
What dreams fill the character's rest?
What family history might be revealed?
What ghost or spirit haunts the character?
What NPC who the character thinks is dead still lives?
What parasite secretly infests the character?
What previous event ties the character to the story?
What ritual was the character blessed with as a child?
What ties the character to this location?
Which family member is involved in the adventure?
Rest of the World Secrets
Use rest of the world secrets to inform the PCs about the larger events happening in the rest world (and to plant seeds for future Threats in Campaign Mode).
PCs might learn these secrets from quest-giving NPCs, notes found on defeated foes, dreams or portents from the gods, NPCs fleeing a disaster, arcane feedback from an object, or psychic projections.
What armies just invaded the realm?
What dark sign or portent just appeared?
What disaster is about to befall the land?
What dungeon entrance just became revealed?
What monsters recently appeared in the realm?
What natural disaster has recently struck the area?
What royal figure was just assassinated?
What unnatural being has appeared in the world?
What unusual creature was seen walking the wilds?
What villainous event will soon come to pass?
Prepare Rewards

Players love treasure, and it's worthwhile to spend time preparing things they'll find interesting. This step also helps to directly impact the characters—by dropping an interesting part of the fiction literally into their hands. You can use a mixture of techniques to prepare these rewards, from generating them randomly to selecting specific items based on the PCs Classes and Paths and the desires of the Players. Treasure pieces are also a great mechanism for delivering secrets and clues.

A Non-Player Character (NPC) is any character that the GM portrays: friends, foes, people, animals, monsters, spirits, or strangers. Each session typically involves various NPCs across different Scenes, which act as the most active part of the adventurer's surroundings.
All NPCs have the following traits:
A Name, maybe of them individually, maybe just of the type of NPC they are collectively, plus what pronouns they use (if applicable)
A Description that summarizes who they are
A Drive that they primarily desire and pursue, be it an instinct, value, emotion, or vow
A short list of Resources that they typically rely on to pursue and achieve their Drive
Additionally, an NPC may have all or any of these traits:
If they have notable defenses or preparations against something, they might Resist some things, meaning they are unaffected by them by default (though this may be overcome narratively)
If they know how to fight, then they’ll have HP, dmg, and Armor

If they're a relevant NPC in the fiction, usually a major antagonist or obstacle, they'll have Conditions that cause Escalations when marked. Each Condition can be emotional or situational, and don't need to be the same as the PCs’ Conditions. When an NPC suffers significant dmg or setback (your call as the GM), you can mark a Condition and have them Escalate, pulling the spotlight back to them and Making the Situation Worse in the process.
Fighting NPCs
When an NPC inflicts dmg, usually from a PC Trading Blows with them, the GM rolls the dmg openly. When an NPC suffers dmg, reduce their HP by that same amount (just as PCs do).

An NPC is defeated when they either reach 0 HP or mark all of their Conditions (after or as part of their final Escalation). NPCs who aren't tough in a fight generally have no HP or dmg, meaning they are defeated after taking a single hit, or even without rolling.

When time passes, such as when the PCs Make Camp, then NPCs can restore some or all of their lost HP and clear their Conditions. You can also restore HP or Conditions in the moment if the fiction fits, such as incredible regeneration abilities, but this should be rare and exceptional.

Creating an NPC Cheat Sheet
Who are they and what do they look like? Write as much or as little of this down as their Description
What core goal or desire do they protect or advance? Write that down as their Drive
What do they use to pursue their Drive? These could be approaches, tools, methods, weapons, or other things; write these down as their Resources
For a dragon this could be teeth, claws, and fire. A merchant might use an always-friendly face, an eye for appraisal, and connections with everyone
What are they particularly defended against or prepared for? Write this down as what they Resist
A knight with a tower shield might Resist: arrows, while a master ranger might Resist: people sneaking up on them in the wilderness
